About

One engine, three visualizers

Stepwise is a small, dependency-free teaching playground for watching algorithms run. Every visualizer here — sorting, pathfinding, and binary search trees — is driven by the same step-player engine. That is the trick that makes the transport bar (play, pause, step forward, step backward, scrub) work identically everywhere, and it is what most home-grown visualizers get wrong.

VISUALIZER 01

Sorting

Six comparison sorts on a bar array, colour-coded by compare, swap, pivot, and sorted, with live counters.

VISUALIZER 02

Pathfinding

BFS, DFS, Dijkstra and A* flood a paintable maze and trace the shortest path. Two maze generators included.

VISUALIZER 03

Binary search tree

Insertions, the three depth-first traversals, and O(h) search — every comparison narrated as it happens.

The record-then-replay model

A naïve visualizer interleaves the algorithm with drawing calls and a setTimeout between each one. That works for "play," but it cannot step backward, cannot scrub to an arbitrary point, and breaks the moment you change speed mid-run. Stepwise avoids all of that by splitting the problem in two:

  • Record. The algorithm runs to completion immediately, on a copy of the data. It never draws anything. Instead, every meaningful event — a comparison, a swap, a cell being visited, a node being placed — is pushed onto a flat array of steps.
  • Replay. The StepPlayer owns an index into that array. Playing just advances the index on a clock; stepping back decrements it; scrubbing sets it directly. A render(index) callback redraws the world for whatever index it is handed.

Because the entire trace exists as plain data before a single frame is drawn, stepping backward is free — there is no need to invert a swap or "un-visit" a cell. You are simply looking at an earlier index. The same is true for scrubbing to step 4,000 of 9,000 instantly.

The full engine lives in js/player.js in about 150 lines. Each visualizer supplies only two things: an array of recorded steps, and a function that draws the state at a given step index. Everything else — the buttons, the scrubber, keyboard shortcuts, the speed control — is shared.

What a step looks like

A step is just a tagged object. The sorting visualizer, for example, emits records like these as it runs:

// inside the recorder, while the sort runs on a copy:
rec.compare(j, j + 1);          // → { type: 'compare', i, j }
if (a[j] > a[j + 1]) rec.swap(j, j + 1);  // → { type: 'swap', i, j }
rec.markSorted(n - 1 - i);      // → { type: 'sorted', indices: [...] }

To draw frame k, the renderer replays the array mutations up to step k (cached as snapshots) and colours each bar by the highlight attached to that step. The live counters — comparisons, swaps, array accesses — are derived from the same trace, so they stay perfectly consistent even when you scrub backward.

Driving the clock

Playback uses requestAnimationFrame with a time accumulator rather than a fixed setInterval. Each frame it adds the elapsed milliseconds to an accumulator and advances as many steps as the chosen speed allows. This keeps playback smooth and frame-rate-independent, and it gracefully catches up (or skips, if you tab away) without drift:

this._acc += dt;
const interval = 1000 / this.speed;   // ms per step
while (this._acc >= interval && !this.atEnd()) {
  this._acc -= interval;
  this.index++;                       // advance one recorded step
}
this.draw();                          // render(this.index)

Correctness first

The point of a teaching tool is that it tells the truth. Every algorithm here is a faithful implementation, not a hand-waved approximation:

  • The six sorts genuinely sort. Merge sort uses an auxiliary buffer and is stable; quick sort uses Lomuto partition around the last element; heap sort builds a real in-place max-heap and sifts down.
  • BFS, Dijkstra and A* return a provably shortest path. A* uses the Manhattan-distance heuristic, which is admissible on a 4-connected grid, so it never overestimates and never returns a sub-optimal route. DFS is included precisely to show a search that does not find the shortest path.
  • Dijkstra and A* expand cells from a binary min-heap (also in player.js's sibling modules), so the cheapest-known cell is always settled first.
  • The BST honours the search-tree invariant on every insert, and an in-order traversal of it always emits the keys in sorted order — you can verify this yourself in the traversal panel.

Built to be opened, not installed

There is no build step, no package manager, and no framework. It is hand-written HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, drawing to a <canvas>. Open index.html from your filesystem and it runs. Your preferred playback speed and colour theme are remembered between visits via localStorage.

Keyboard: Space play / pause · ← → step a single instruction · Home / End jump to the first or last step. Everything is reachable by Tab, and the whole thing respects prefers-reduced-motion — if you have it on, nothing auto-animates and you drive each step yourself.

Where to go next

Try the same array in bubble sort versus quick sort and compare the comparison counts. Generate a maze in the pathfinding lab and run A* against BFS to see how much less of the grid A* needs to explore. Or insert the keys 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 into the binary tree to watch a degenerate, linked-list-shaped tree form — then hit "Balanced" to see the difference height makes.

Stepwise is a fictional educational project created as a self-contained demo. The algorithms, complexities, and behaviours described above are real and correct.
